title: How satyagraha got its name
hookLine: can you stand up to someone without hating them? a new word, and a sermon
carry: satyagraha: hold firm to truth, without hate
tomorrow: what's inside not-harming, the way Gandhi read it?

cards: Standing up to someone usually comes with heat: the clenched jaw, the comeback, the wish to see them lose. So here's the question: can a person stand up to someone without hating them?
A young lawyer in South Africa thought so, and his struggle needed a name. People called it passive resistance. Mohandas Gandhi didn't like the phrase.

teach.b: In his book Satyagraha in South Africa, he tells how the new name was found. Passive resistance, he felt, sounded like a weapon of the weak and left room for hatred. His newspaper asked readers for a better word.
His cousin Maganlal sent in sadagraha, firmness in a good cause, and Gandhi shaped it into satyagraha. Satya, truth.
Agraha, holding firm. Holding on to truth, without harming the other side to win. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you."
Gandhi wrote in his autobiography that the Sermon on the Mount went straight to his heart, and that he read it alongside the Gita.
Later, a Baptist pastor in Alabama, Martin Luther King Jr., wrote that his nonviolence took its spirit from Jesus and its method from Gandhi.
Shared: answering harm without returning it, and refusing to hate the person in front of you. And an honest difference. For King, that love comes from following Jesus.
Gandhi stayed a Hindu, and the aim he named was truth: he worshiped God as Truth.
Two starting points, and a long stretch of shared road.

how: Gandhi's autobiography and Satyagraha in South Africa, read in homes and classrooms, are where he tells in his own words how truth and nonviolence became a way of public life.

o: two rival leaders who argued over the meaning of the Gita
a Hindu teacher and his student in South Africa
a Hindu leader and a Christian leader joined by nonviolence

games.q: one word, two roots. tap the pairs.
p: spirit from Jesus, method from Gandhi

s: Gandhi named his movement passive resistance and kept that name
he disliked it and found a new word: satyagraha.
Gandhi wrote that the Sermon on the Mount went straight to his heart
and he read it alongside the Gita.
satyagraha and Christian love are simply the same thing
they share ground; King's love comes from following Jesus, Gandhi's aim was truth.

games.q: a classmate says nonviolence is just being passive. what would Gandhi's own word answer?
o: he agreed; that's why he called it passive resistance.
satyagraha: holding firm to truth, without hatred.
games.why: Gandhi dropped 'passive resistance' because it sounded weak and left room for hatred. satyagraha holds firm, and still doesn't hate.

practice: Listen for one steady sound near you: a fan, traffic, your own breath. Let it be firm and unhurried.
Bring to mind someone you're at odds with, and for a few breaths hold two things at once: what's true, and no wish to see them harmed.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi and King: a Hindu lawyer and a Baptist pastor, joined by satyagraha, holding firm to truth without hatred.

orig.note: a word shaped by Gandhi from Sanskrit: satya, truth; agraha, holding firm.

carryVoice: Your line: satyagraha, hold firm to truth, without hate. Quiet can still be strong. See you tomorrow.
